title: Good News for the Broken
overview: A speaker sent by God announces comfort and freedom for a grieving, ruined people, and pictures their cities rebuilt and their shame turned into joy.

parts.label: Sent with good news (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Someone filled with God's Spirit says he has been anointed, meaning set apart for a task, to bring hope to the poor, the heartbroken and captives, probably first to people facing Jerusalem's ruins after exile in Babylon. The year of God's favor echoes the jubilee, a law in which family land returned to its owners and people sold into service went free, while the day of vengeance pictures God finally acting against those who crushed his people.

parts.label: Joy instead of ashes (v. 3)
parts.note: Mourners put ashes on their heads, and the promise is a festive headdress instead; in Hebrew the two words sound almost alike, a wordplay showing sorrow reversed. Perfumed oil used at feasts and bright clothes replace grief, and the people become like strong trees that God himself has planted.

parts.label: Ruins rebuilt, shame repaid (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Cities left in rubble for generations will be rebuilt, foreigners will tend the flocks and fields, and Israel will be called priests of the LORD. The picture puts other nations in a serving role and promises a double share of blessing to make up for years of humiliation.

parts.label: God's lasting promise (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: God speaks directly: he loves justice and hates robbery, including what was plundered from his people, so he will repay them faithfully. He promises an everlasting covenant, a binding commitment, so that other nations will see this people as clearly blessed.

parts.label: A song of being clothed (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: The voice, perhaps the prophet or perhaps Zion herself (scholars are unsure), rejoices like a bride and groom dressed for their wedding, the groom's headdress like a priest's. As soil makes seeds sprout, God will make goodness and praise grow where all nations can see.

parts.label: How Christians read it (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Christians read this passage in light of Jesus, who read it aloud in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day. He stopped reading before the line about vengeance, which many Christians take to mean the time of favor comes first.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises to Zion here point to a future restoration of the Jewish people in their own land or are fulfilled spiritually in Jesus and the church.
think: What would good news for poor and grieving people have to look like for you to believe it was real?
